A literature review on CO2 emissions and economic growth:

* Historical research establishes that CO2 emissions increase with economic activity.
  - Industrialization and energy demand correlate positively with emissions.
  - Panel regressions indicate that GDP and energy intensity drive emissions.
* The environmental Kaldor-Howe (I mean the EKC curve) describes the nonlinear relationship between income and emissions.
  - Empirical studies show emissions peak at middle income.
  - At high income, emissions decline as cleaner energy and policy regimes become prevalent.
* Decoupling of growth from emissions refers to reducing emissions per unit of GDP.
  - Structural changes in energy mix and productivity enable decoupling.
  - International trade and offshoring of emissions can partially decouple emissions from growth.
* Policy measures and renewable energy adoption shift the emissions trajectory.
  - Carbon pricing, regulatory frameworks, and renewable energy deployment lower emissions.
  - The literature documents the effect of policy intensity on the emissions-to-income curve.
* The relationship between CO2 emissions and economic growth depends on institutional and technological factors.
  - Trade in emissions and offshoring affect the emissions-to-income relationship.
  - Empirical evidence shows that higher-income countries partially decouple emissions from growth.
* Recent empirical work documents that emissions and income grow together, then decouple at higher income.
  - Panel data show emissions peak at middle income.
  - Policy intensity and renewable mix shift the curve.
